description: Mid streaming recognition track. Module 5 of 5 — reading mid-level streaming pipelines.

tasks.title: Audit a Mid-Level Streaming Pipeline

description.context: A NordGrid Mid engineer claims they built a stateful streaming pipeline that aggregates per-meter consumption, dedupes by event_id, exactly-once writes to Delta, and runs at 250K-meter scale. They show the senior the pipeline AND the resulting RocksDB metrics and ask for review. The senior asks the engineer to verify EACH design decision by reading the metrics — not by trusting the configuration. Five sub-questions audit five different aspects.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 60-line stateful streaming pipeline at NordGrid Mid scale; verify each Mid-level streaming concept against the metrics

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# NordGrid Mid stateful streaming pipeline

schema = StructType([
    StructField('event_id',   StringType()),
    StructField('meter_id',   StringType()),
    StructField('event_time', TimestampType()),
    StructField('region',     StringType()),
    StructField('kw',         DoubleType())])

raw = (spark.readStream.format('kafka')
         .option('subscribe', 'nordgrid.meters')
         .option('startingOffsets', 'earliest')
         .load())

parsed = raw.select(from_json(col('value').cast('string'), schema).alias('e')).select('e.*')

# Stage 1: dedupe by event_id (handle producer retries)
deduped = (parsed.withWatermark('event_time', '15 minutes')
                 .dropDuplicates(['event_id', 'event_time']))

# Stage 2: per-meter rolling 1-hour total
rolling = (deduped.withWatermark('event_time', '15 minutes')
                  .groupBy(window('event_time', '1 hour'), 'meter_id')
                  .agg(sum('kw').alias('total_kw')))

# Stage 3: write to Delta
q = (rolling.writeStream
        .outputMode('update')
        .format('delta')
        .option('checkpointLocation', 's3://nordgrid/ckpt/rolling')
        .option('path', 's3://nordgrid/silver/meters_rolling')
        .trigger(processingTime='30 seconds')
        .start())

# RocksDB state-store metrics (steady-state, hour 12)
# numRowsTotal:        ~280,000
# numRowsUpdated:      ~95 per batch
# numRowsRemoved:      ~80 per batch
# stateStoreSizeBytes: 2.4 GB
#
# StreamingQueryProgress
# inputRowsPerSecond:     5,000
# processedRowsPerSecond: 5,200 (slight catch-up margin)
# avg batch duration:    9 seconds (well under 30s trigger)

fields.label: Q1 — Did the dropDuplicates with watermark engage cleanup correctly?
options: Yes — readStream + format('kafka') + startingOffsets='earliest' replays the topic backlog at startup. Appropriate for cold-start initialization but may cause a multi-day catch-up window for large topics.
No — dropDuplicates with two-column key (event_id, event_time) is forbidden in Spark 3.5; only single-column keys work with watermarks. State will grow until the next major release.
Yes, but only because event_id has high cardinality. With low-cardinality keys, dropDuplicates leaks state regardless of watermark. The pattern works here by coincidence.
Yes — dedupe key includes event_time, so the watermark can expire entries whose event_time falls below it. numRowsRemoved being non-zero (~80/batch) confirms cleanup is firing. State stays bounded.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — dedupe key includes event_time, so the watermark can expire entries whose event_time falls below it. numRowsRemoved being non-zero (~80/batch) confirms cleanup is firing. State stays bounded.
fields.rationale: dropDuplicates(['event_id', 'event_time']) makes the dedupe key event-time-aware.Spark expires entries whose event_time falls below the watermark.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats watermark as drop-only; it drives both drops and state cleanup when the key is event-time-aware.

fields.label: Q2 — Does Stage 2's windowed aggregation cooperate properly with the watermark?
options: Yes — groupBy(window('event_time', '1 hour'), 'meter_id') gives every per-meter entry a window-bound time component. Watermark expires entries when window close + tolerance falls below.
No — applying withWatermark twice in one query (once in Stage 1, once in Stage 2) is illegal. Spark uses only the first call and ignores Stage 2's call entirely.
Yes, but the 1-hour window is too coarse for 250K meters. Reduce to 1-minute windows so state stays below 10K total entries instead of growing larger.
No — windowed aggregation requires append output mode for watermark cleanup. update mode bypasses cleanup; switch to append for state to bound itself properly.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — groupBy(window('event_time', '1 hour'), 'meter_id') gives every per-meter entry a window-bound time component. Watermark expires entries when window close + tolerance falls below.
fields.rationale: Per-meter entries gain time-bound expiry via the window-based grouping pattern used here.
fields.distractorRationale: Option B: Invents an illegal-double-withWatermark rule; both calls are valid.

fields.label: Q3 — Does the Delta sink with checkpointLocation provide exactly-once semantics here?
options: No — Delta provides at-least-once only by default; for exactly-once add foreachBatch with manual MERGE INTO logic keyed on batch_id explicitly.
Yes — the lakehouse-native sink format integrates its transaction log directly into the engine's offset tracking. End-to-end de-duplication is automatic.
Yes, but only if .option('mergeSchema', 'true') is set. Without it, restarts skip the schema-evolution check and may write duplicates if columns drifted.
Exactly-once is impossible with update mode; only append mode achieves exactly-once on Delta. Switch to append plus a windowed-only schema setup.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — the lakehouse-native sink format integrates its transaction log directly into the engine's offset tracking. End-to-end de-duplication is automatic.
fields.rationale: Built-in lakehouse sinks couple atomic commit semantics on the output side with checkpointed offset tracking on the input side via a single internal.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats Delta as at-least-once only; Delta is exactly-once via transaction log.

fields.label: Q4 — Are throughput and trigger configured appropriately?
options: No — processedRowsPerSecond 5,200 > inputRowsPerSecond 5,000 means the cluster is over-provisioned; downsize executors to save money. The 9s batch with 30s trigger wastes 21s of cluster idle time per cycle.

Yes — input rate 5,000/sec, processed rate 5,200/sec means slight margin. Average batch 9s with 30s trigger gives breathing room. Trigger could be tightened for fresher data, but 30s is safe production.
No — trigger='30 seconds' creates 30-second average latency from event arrival to Delta write. For SCADA monitoring, sub-second latency is required. Switch to continuous-mode trigger.
No — 30s trigger is too tight for 9s batch; Spark recommends trigger ≥ 3× batch duration as a guideline. Increase to 60s for batch stability and recovery margin.
fields.correctAnswer: Yes — input rate 5,000/sec, processed rate 5,200/sec means slight margin. Average batch 9s with 30s trigger gives breathing room. Trigger could be tightened for fresher data, but 30s is safe production.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats minor headroom as over-provisioning; you want headroom for spikes.

fields.label: Q5 — Looking at the full pipeline, what is the largest residual risk that could break exactly-once or state cleanup despite the apparently-correct configuration?
options: The 15-minute watermark in Stage 1 is identical to Stage 2 — if the engineer later changes ONE without the other, the cross-stage watermark contract breaks subtly. Document the watermark coordination requirement.

Delta's auto-compaction (run by Operations on a separate schedule) could conflict with the streaming write checkpoint, causing duplicate rows. Disable Delta auto-compaction on s3://nordgrid/silver/meters_rolling.

If a new column is added to the upstream Kafka schema without restarting the streaming query, parsed.select('e.*') will silently drop the new column. The query continues but loses data; not visible in metrics.

Risk of late events arriving more than 15 minutes after their event_time. Late events are dropped by both watermarks. Monitor 'numRowsDroppedByWatermark' to track late-event rate and adjust if drops exceed acceptable levels.
fields.correctAnswer: If a new column is added to the upstream Kafka schema without restarting the streaming query, parsed.select('e.*') will silently drop the new column. The query continues but loses data; not visible in metrics.
fields.rationale: Schema drift is the silent risk.*') uses the schema declared at query start time.*') only sees the columns it knows about.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats watermark coordination as residual; the engineer's PR review captures this risk.

tasks.title: Five Missed Streaming Opportunities

description.context: Final STI exercise. A NordGrid pipeline runs but is suboptimal at the streaming level. The senior asks the engineer to read both the pipeline AND its observed state-store metrics and identify FIVE missed streaming opportunities. Each one is a different category covered by Modules 1-4: stateful design, watermark + cleanup, exactly-once sink, throughput tuning, output mode choice. The pipeline LOOKS reasonable; the engineer must connect each metric symptom to its cause.
description.task: Read the artifact above, then answer the questions in order.

evidence.title: Dataset
evidence.content: 60-line streaming pipeline at NordGrid Mid scale with 5 embedded missed-optimization opportunities

evidence.label: Plan output
evidence.content:
# Pipeline as written
schema = StructType([
    StructField('event_id', StringType()),
    StructField('meter_id', StringType()),
    StructField('event_time', TimestampType()),
    StructField('region', StringType()),
    StructField('kw', DoubleType())])

raw = (spark.readStream.format('kafka')
         .option('subscribe', 'nordgrid.meters').load())

parsed = raw.select(from_json(col('value').cast('string'), schema).alias('e')).select('e.*')

# Stage 1: dedupe by event_id alone
deduped = parsed.dropDuplicates(['event_id'])

# Stage 2: per-meter total (no time bucket)
rolling = (deduped.withWatermark('event_time', '5 minutes')
                  .groupBy('meter_id').sum('kw'))

# Stage 3: write via foreachBatch with plain INSERT
def write_to_postgres(df, batch_id):
    df.write.format('jdbc').option('url', '...').option('dbtable', 'metrics').mode('append').save()

q = (rolling.writeStream
        .outputMode('complete')
        .foreachBatch(write_to_postgres)
        .trigger(processingTime='5 seconds')
        .start())

# Observed metrics (steady-state, hour 24)
# RocksDB numRowsTotal:    340,000 and growing linearly
# RocksDB numRowsRemoved:  0 every batch
# inputRowsPerSecond:      5,000
# processedRowsPerSecond:  3,200
# avg batch duration:      8 seconds (vs 5s trigger)
# Postgres metrics table:  duplicate rows after every restart
# Driver heap:             3.2 GB and growing

fields.label: Q1 — Missed Opportunity #1: Stage 1 dedupes by event_id alone (no event_time). What is the symptom and fix?
options: RocksDB state grows because event_id has no event-time component for watermark to expire. Every event_id ever seen stays. Fix: dropDuplicates(['event_id', 'event_time']).
event_id deduplication is broken in Spark 3.5; switch to a manual GROUP BY event_id, MAX(event_time) approach with custom aggregation logic added.
dropDuplicates without watermark is the issue; the withWatermark in Stage 2 is too late to fire on Stage 1's state cleanup. Move the withWatermark before Stage 1 entirely to fix.
Spark's dropDuplicates only works on numeric columns; event_id as string causes silent state leak. Cast event_id to a hash int first to fix the leak issue.
fields.correctAnswer: RocksDB state grows because event_id has no event-time component for watermark to expire. Every event_id ever seen stays. Fix: dropDuplicates(['event_id', 'event_time']).
fields.rationale: dropDuplicates(['event_id']) holds state for every distinct event_id forever.
fields.distractorRationale: 5 bug; dropDuplicates works correctly with the right key.

fields.label: Q2 — Missed Opportunity #2: Stage 2 uses groupBy('meter_id') — no time bucket. Why is this another state leak path?
options: groupBy meter_id has no event-time component for cleanup. Watermark cannot expire per-meter state. Fix is groupBy window event_time, meter_id.
groupBy on a single string column always leaks state in streaming. Use groupBy on a numeric column instead to fix the issue properly.
The 5-minute watermark is too short — increase it to 1 hour and state will stabilize naturally without other code changes needed.
Per-meter aggregation requires mapGroupsWithState explicitly; built-in aggregations cannot be cleaned up under any watermark.
fields.correctAnswer: groupBy meter_id has no event-time component for cleanup. Watermark cannot expire per-meter state. Fix is groupBy window event_time, meter_id.
fields.rationale: 2 — groupBy without a time-bound key cannot use the watermark for per-key cleanup.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Invents a string-column-leaks-state rule.
Option C: Treats watermark threshold as the problem; key shape is.

fields.label: Q3 — Missed Opportunity #3: foreachBatch with .mode('append') and no batch_id key. What is the symptom?
options: Append mode is slower than overwrite for small batches; switch to overwrite for performance gains. Duplicates are unrelated to the mode choice here.
JDBC sinks do not support exactly-once natively; switch to Delta. Duplicates will disappear once the sink format is changed completely.
Postgres ALWAYS deduplicates on insert via its own constraints; the duplicates observed are a Postgres bug, not a Spark issue at all.
Append-mode writes are non-idempotent. Partial writes remain in Postgres; replay writes the same rows again. Fix: include batch_id with overwrite semantics.
fields.correctAnswer: Append-mode writes are non-idempotent. Partial writes remain in Postgres; replay writes the same rows again. Fix: include batch_id with overwrite semantics.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option A: Invents Postgres dedup; not how INSERT INTO works.
Option B: Treats it as a performance issue; duplicates are the symptom.

fields.label: Q4 — Missed Opportunity #4: trigger='5 seconds' but batches take 8 seconds. What is the symptom and fix?
options: Batches run back-to-back since 8s exceeds the 5s trigger. Source falls behind: input 5,000 vs processed 3,200. Fix is throughput-side. Trigger interval alone does not fix the gap.
The 5s trigger is fine; Spark internally batches whenever ready. The processedRate < inputRate gap is a metric-reporting artifact and self-corrects within 24 hours.
5s trigger forces continuous-mode execution implicitly, which has lower throughput than micro-batch. Set trigger='30 seconds' to switch back to micro-batch mode.
Increase trigger to 30 seconds; with longer trigger windows, each batch processes more events and throughput recovers automatically without scaling executors.
fields.correctAnswer: Batches run back-to-back since 8s exceeds the 5s trigger. Source falls behind: input 5,000 vs processed 3,200. Fix is throughput-side. Trigger interval alone does not fix the gap.
fields.rationale: Trigger interval is a TIMING control, not a THROUGHPUT control.inputRate 5,000/sec, processedRate 3,200/sec means a 1,800-event-per-second deficit.
fields.distractorRationale:
Option B: Treats throughput gap as metric artifact; it is real.
Option C: Invents continuous-mode auto-switch; Spark stays in micro-batch.

fields.label: Q5 — Missed Opportunity #5: outputMode('complete') with growing per-meter state. Combined effect with Q1-Q4 — which fix has the largest impact?
options: Q3 fix (foreachBatch idempotency) — duplicates are visible to downstream consumers, the most user-visible problem. Largest business impact even though state issues are technically larger by absolute size.
Q4 fix (scale executors) — fixes throughput which addresses lag, indirectly slowing state growth because fewer events accumulate. The single most-impactful change.
Q5 fix (switch to update mode) — complete mode re-emits all 340K rows every batch, keeping driver heap at 3.2GB AND making batches slow. Update mode addresses heap and batch duration both.
Q1 fix (dedupe key) — the dedupe leak is the largest absolute state, so fixing it most directly bounds RocksDB. All other fixes are secondary in business impact.
fields.correctAnswer: Q5 fix (switch to update mode) — complete mode re-emits all 340K rows every batch, keeping driver heap at 3.2GB AND making batches slow. Update mode addresses heap and batch duration both.
fields.rationale: Re-emission cost dominates batch duration when state grows alongside output retention requirements.2 GB heap pressure.
fields.distractorRationale: Option A: Treats user-visibility as architectural priority; state issues compound technically.
